criterion_scores.reasoning: I checked the advertised rubric/version behavior against the actual defaults and prompt instructions (lines 3-5, 16-18, 36-38, 44-51) as well as the main API flow (53-80). The HTTP/request path is serviceable, but the script's core contract is undermined by pinning the default rubric to v3 and hardcoding build-quality@3 scoring logic in the prompt.

I checked whether the script covers the end-to-end judge flow: args, preflight checks, request build, API call, console output, and log write (19-35, 53-105). Those parts are present, but an obvious failure case is unhandled cleanly: value-taking flags can crash on missing $2 instead of producing a proper usage error (line 21 and similar cases).

I checked file placement/naming and source-of-truth discipline, especially around logged eval fields (1-18, 89-105). Placement is conventional, but logging model-provided weighted_score/verdict directly at line 102 breaks the house convention that derived adjudication fields should come from a single deterministic source.

I looked for duplicated policy logic, over-delegation to the model, and brittle prompt-only behavior (44-51, 82-104). The script duplicates rubric arithmetic/caps inside prompt text and asks the model to compute composite/verdict, which is exactly the kind of split-responsibility pattern that drifts and is hard to audit.

I checked hard-failure messages, network-error visibility, and response validation depth (33-35, 67-80). There are decent preflight errors for missing files/keys, but curl stderr is suppressed and the verdict JSON validation is too shallow to make malformed responses legible or safely rejected.

defects.description: The script advertises judging against the current build-quality rubric with version derived from the file, but the default rubric path is pinned to v3. Once repo defaults move forward, callers who do not override --rubric silently evaluate against stale rules.

defects.quote: Compute raw = correctness*0.30 + completeness*0.20 + convention_adherence*0.20 + anti_pattern_avoidance*0.20 + diagnostics*0.10 (round 3 dp). THEN apply build-quality@3 caps to get the final weighted_score: if the artifact asserts an unverified/uncited claim as verified, set confidence_honesty_violation=true and cap weighted_score<=0.65; if it references a load-bearing file that does not exist, cap<=0.60; if a command only lists agents without dispatch/output, cap<=0.35. verdict="pass" if final weighted_score>=0.70 else "flag".'
defects.description: Scoring logic and caps are hardcoded to build-quality@3 inside the model prompt. That means changing --rubric only changes the attached text and logged rubric version, not the operative instructions the model follows, which contradicts the script's version-derived/current-rubric framing.

The script asks the model to produce deterministic derived fields (weighted_score and verdict) instead of keeping arithmetic and pass/fail logic in code/harness. That duplicates policy logic in prompt text and creates a brittle split source of truth.

The run log persists model-supplied weighted_score and verdict as authoritative fields rather than recomputing them from criterion_scores locally. That violates source-of-truth discipline and lets model arithmetic/schema mistakes become logged truth.

defects.quote: echo "$VERDICT_JSON" | jq -e '.criterion_scores | length == 5' >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "ERROR: malformed verdict JSON:" >&2; echo "$VERDICT_JSON" | head -c 600 >&2; exit 1; }
defects.description: Validation is shallow: it checks only that criterion_scores has length 5. It does not verify score ranges, expected ids, presence/types of weighted_score or verdict, or even that the object shape beyond that field is correct.
curl stderr is discarded, which makes transport- or TLS-level failures harder to diagnose. The later HTTP-code check helps, but request-construction/network errors lose useful detail.

Options that require a value assume $2 exists. If a caller supplies a flag without its argument, set -u will terminate with a shell-level unbound-variable error instead of a controlled usage message for this obvious failure case.
